semantic_correction.stem: A healthy adult asks the nurse for general guidance about daily hydration. Which response is accurate?

options.A: Water needs vary with factors such as activity and environment, and fluids from beverages and water-rich foods contribute to intake.
options.B: Every healthy adult needs the same fixed amount of plain water each day regardless of activity, pregnancy status, or climate.
options.C: Water from foods contributes little to daily intake, so hydration guidance should count plain drinking water and other beverages alone.
options.D: Hot weather and increased physical activity generally lower water needs because the body conserves fluid more efficiently under stress.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC guidance updated March 5, 2026 states that daily water-intake recommendations vary with factors including age, sex, pregnancy status, breastfeeding status, and activity level. The body needs more water in hot climates and when more physically active. Daily water intake comes mostly from water and other beverages, while foods—especially water-rich fruits and vegetables—also add to fluid intake. Therefore option A correctly reflects individualized hydration rather than a universal fixed volume.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach that hydration needs are individualized and that total daily water intake includes fluids from beverages and foods, with needs increasing in heat and with greater physical activity.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
semantic_correction.source_locator: Your body needs more water when you are — hot climates and more physically active. Meeting your water intake every day — recommendations vary by age, sex, pregnancy status, activity level, and breastfeeding status; water and other beverages provide most intake and foods with high water content also contribute
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: CDC states that water needs vary by individual and environmental factors, increase with heat and activity, and are met through both beverages and water-containing foods.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: shortened the keyed response, balanced all choices, and retained CDC's individualized-needs, heat/activity, and food/fluid contribution principles without inventing one universal volume target.

audit_findings_append.source_locator: About Water and Healthier Drinks, updated March 5, 2026
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — hydration education
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests individualized hydration and total-fluid sources without a correct-answer length cue or unsupported fixed-volume recommendation.

option_audit.A: Correct. It directly reflects CDC guidance on variable needs and contributions from beverages and foods.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. CDC states that needs vary by multiple individual and environmental factors.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Water-rich foods can contribute meaningfully to total fluid intake.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. CDC states that hot climates and increased physical activity increase water needs.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone correctly combines individualized requirements and all major sources of daily water intake.
cueing_check: All four options are hydration-guidance statements of comparable length and specificity; no unique-length or absolute-word cue identifies A.
